CLINICALTRIALS: gov/study/NCT04083859.

title: Camrelizumab plus chemotherapy as induction therapy followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy and camrelizumab consolidation in limited-stage small cell lung cancer: a randomized phase II trial.
authors: Liu D, Yang L, Hu M et al.
abstract: Definitive chemoradiotherapy followed by immunotherapy consolidation is the current standard of care for limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC). We conducted a randomized phase II trial (ChiCTR2000032275) to evaluate a camrelizumab-based induction-consolidation strategy in previously untreated patients with LS-SCLC. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive induction camrelizumab plus etoposide-platinum followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) and camrelizumab consolidation (camrelizumab group), or induction chemotherapy followed by concurrent CRT alone (cCRT group). The primary endpoint was the 1‑year progression‑free survival (PFS) rate. Secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. Between November 2020 and April 2024, 41 patients were enrolled. At a median follow‑up of 32.1 months (interquartile range [IQR]: 26.4-38.7), ORR was 100% in the camrelizumab group and 83.3% in the cCRT group. The 1‑year PFS rates were 65.5% with camrelizumab versus 47.4% with cCRT (P = 0.029). Median PFS was 24.0 months versus 11.8 months, and median OS was not reached versus 23.9 months (P = 0.042). Exploratory biomarker analyses indicated that patients with lower baseline systemic inflammatory indices, including neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio <2.8 and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio <207.0, and those with a decline in lactate dehydrogenase at week 12 after CRT, derived greater benefit from camrelizumab. The OS benefit was also more evident in patients with Ki-67 ≤80%. Toxicities in the camrelizumab group were manageable, with a low incidence of severe immune-related adverse events (4.8%), and radiation pneumonitis rates were comparable between groups. Taken together, induction camrelizumab combined with chemotherapy, followed by CRT and camrelizumab consolidation, significantly improved survival outcomes in LS-SCLC, with a manageable safety profile, warranting further validation for this aggressive malignancy.

title: [Imaging of pulmonary nodules: A diagnostic approach].
authors: Khalil A, Denguir H, Gounant V et al.
abstract: The detection of pulmonary nodules has increased considerably with the widespread use of chest-computed tomography and the development of low-dose CT lung cancer screening. The pulmonary nodule represents a major diagnostic challenge, requiring rigorous evaluation in order to distinguish benign from malignant lesions while limiting unnecessary invasive investigations. Analysis relies on precise morphological characterization (density, size, margins), assessment of persistence and growth over time, and integration of the clinical context. The Fleischner Society guidelines and the protocols derived from organized screening programs now form the basis of standardized management. This article provides a detailed review of the radiological criteria, decision-making algorithms, and the role of transthoracic needle biopsy in the management of pulmonary nodules.

title: A Novel TCP and NTCP Modeling Framework Incorporating Inter-Fractional Deviations and Biological Effectiveness for Hyper-fractionated Radiotherapy.
authors: Kong X, Fu X, Yu J et al.
journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
abstract:
PURPOSE: High-dose hyper-fractionated radiotherapy has been recently included in NCCN guidelines for limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC), which clinical outcomes are dependent on actually delivered biologically effective dose (BED). However, most tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models rely on planed physical dose without considering inter-fractional deviations and BED of fractionization. This study aims to develop TCP and NTCP models for LS-SCLC incorporating CBCT-based inter-fractional anatomies and hyper-fractional radiobiological dose.
METHODS AND MATERIALS: Inter-fractional dose was accumulated based on deformable image registration between CBCT and planning CT (pCT). Both TCP and NTCP were formulated within a BED-based framework, using dose-volume parameters calculated from planned dose and CBCT-based accumulated dose for comparison. The LQ model with "4R" effects and Gompertzian tumor growth (LQRG) and Lyman-Kutcher-Burman (LKB) models were used for TCP and NTCP modeling. Based on the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), negative log-likelihood (NLL), and Akaike information criterion (AIC), model performances were assessed for local progression-free survival (LPFS), radiation pneumonitis and radiation esophagitis.
RESULTS: Compared with pCT dose, CBCT dose showed superior discrimination of normal tissue toxicity. For grade ≥2 radiation pneumonitis, the CBCT-based NTCP model achieved significantly higher AUC (0.67 vs. 0.59) and lower NLL (62.39 vs. 66.13) than that of the pCT-based mode. Superiority of CBCT-based NTCP model was also observed for grade ≥3 radiation esophagitis, i.e., AUC (0.62 vs. 0.58) and NLL (55.55 vs. 56.64). Using the observed LPFS as reference, marginally improved TCP modeling was observed using CBCT dose than that of pCT, where the AUC values were 0.80 vs. 0.79 (GTV 45 Gy) and 0.77 vs. 0.75 (GTV 54 Gy).
CONCLUSIONS: By incorporating inter-fractional deviation and biological effectiveness, the improved accuracy of TCP and NTCP models provides preliminary evidence supporting the treatment planning and toxicity management for LS-SCLC patients treated with the hyper-fractionated radiotherapy, which needs further clinical validation.

title: American Radium Society Appropriate Use Criteria: Accelerated hypofractionated radiotherapy in the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced non-small cell lung cancer ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy.
authors: Chun SG, Iyengar P, Rimner A et al.
journal: Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: While accelerated hypofractionated radiotherapy has increasingly been adopted in the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy, there is a paucity of randomized prospective evidence guiding utilization. Given the marked heterogeneity in the presentations of locally-advanced NSCLC, the American Radium Society (ARS) Thoracic Appropriate Use Criteria (AUC) Panel evaluated the appropriateness of accelerated hypofractionation in the context of multidisciplinary management.
METHODS: Five clinical variants representing manifestations of locally-advanced NSCLC were developed by the 15-member multidisciplinary ARS Thoracic AUC panel. The English-language medical literature was formally reviewed from 2010-2025 and scrutinized for prospective clinical trials utilizing accelerated hypofractionation for concurrent chemotherapy ineligible patients. All case variants were evaluated with respect to use of radiation technique, radiation fractionation, and utilization of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy with Modified Delphi methodology. Consensus recommendations were reviewed and approved by the ARS Executive Committee and subject to public comment.
RESULTS: The literature review identified 228 articles, of which there were 14 prospective trials/registries including nine Phase I-II trials, four prospective registries, and one randomized Phase III trial. There was consensus that it is appropriate to utilize intensity modulated radiation therapy and proton therapy across presentations of locally-advanced NSCLC, with the aim of constraining the lung V20Gy<30% and heart V40Gy<20% with accelerated hypofractionation. When utilizing 15-fraction accelerated hypofractionation for disease abutting the esophagus or brachial plexus, there was consensus that it is inappropriate to exceed doses of 45-55 Gy. With respect to PD-L1 immunotherapy, there was consensus that consolidative immunotherapy after definitive radiation therapy is appropriate, but that concurrent immunotherapy is inappropriate. There was panel consensus that it may be appropriate to utilize induction PD-L1 immunotherapy prior to radiation therapy in cases of bulky or N3 disease to test disease biology. Across variants, there was consensus that conventionally fractionated radiotherapy to 60 Gy in 30 fractions remains appropriate.
CONCLUSIONS: The ARS Thoracic AUC Panel has provided consensus case-based guidelines on the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced NSCLC ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy reflecting the heterogeneity of disease presentation in this population. In absence of randomized prospective data demonstrating superiority of accelerated hypofractionation, conventionally fractionated radiotherapy remains an appropriate option.

title: Application of a concise video to improve patient understanding of tumor genomic testing in community and academic practice settings.
authors: Veney DJ, Wei L, Miller J et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Tumor genomic testing (TGT) is standard-of-care for most patients with advanced/metastatic cancer. Despite established guidelines, patient education prior to TGT is frequently omitted. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the impact and durability of a concise 3-4 minute video for patient education prior to TGT in community versus academic sites and across cancer types.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients undergoing standard-of-care TGT were enrolled at a tertiary academic institution in three cohorts: Cohort 1-breast cancer; Cohort 2-lung cancer; Cohort 3-other cancers. Cohort 4 consisted of patients with any cancer type similarly undergoing SOC TGT at one of three community cancer centers. Participants completed survey measures prior to video viewing (T1), immediately post-viewing (T2), and after return of TGT results (T3). Outcome measures included: 1) 10-question objective genomic knowledge/understanding (GKU); 2) 10-question video message-specific knowledge (VMSK); 3) 11-question Trust in Physician/Provider (TIPP); 4) perceptions regarding TGT.
RESULTS: A total of 203 participants completed all survey timepoints. Higher baseline GKU and VMSK scores were significantly associated with higher income and greater years of education. For the primary objective, there was a significant and sustained improvement in VMSK from T1:T2:T3 (Poverall p < 0.0001), with no significant change in GKU (p = 0.41) or TIPP (p = 0.73). This trend was consistent within each cohort (all p ≤ 0.0001). Results for four VMSK questions significantly improved, including impact on treatment decisions, incidental germline findings, and insurance coverage of testing.
CONCLUSIONS: A concise, 3-4 minute, broadly applicable educational video administered prior to TGT significantly and sustainably improved video message-specific knowledge in diverse cancer types and in academic and community settings. This resource is publicly available at http://www.tumor-testing.com, with a goal to efficiently educate and empower patients regarding TGT while addressing guidelines within the flow of clinical practice.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05215769.

title: "What's the point?": A Case Report on Music Therapy and Terminal Cancer.
authors: Davenport V
abstract: Palliative care (PC) helps to improve quality of life and alleviate suffering for those who are faced with a terminal cancer diagnosis. Music therapy (MT) is a type of expressive arts therapy that may be beneficial for PC patients to help manage physical symptoms as well as address psychosocial, spiritual, and existential needs. The present case report explores the use of MT as an existential form of therapy with Joe, a PC patient with terminal lung cancer. MT addressed Joe's physical and psychosocial needs and provided space to explore existential topics related to death and dying, ultimately leading to transcendence and acceptance.

title: Single-Cell Transcriptomics Identifies Fibroblast-Associated Transcriptional Patterns and Candidate Therapeutic Targets in the Comorbidity of Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer and Obesity.
authors: Yuan J, Yu S, Zheng J
abstract:
BACKGROUND/INTRODUCTION: Obesity acts as a critical modifiable risk factor for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), while the key cellular and molecular drivers mediating their comorbid association remain poorly defined. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables precise resolution of cell-specific transcriptomic features, making it an optimal tool for uncovering inter-disease regulatory patterns.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: scRNA-seq datasets for NSCLC (GSE198099, 2 tumor/2 normal samples) and obesity (GSE214982, 5 obese/4 lean samples) were obtained from GEO and processed using Seurat (v5.x). Cell types were annotated by SingleR and validated with canonical lineage markers. Intercellular communication was inferred using CellChat (v2.x) with the human ligand-receptor database. Shared differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified and validated by bulk RNA-seq (GSE21933 and GSE55200). Functional enrichment, protein-protein interaction network, and drug-gene interaction analyses were integrated to identify repurposable FDA-approved agents.
RESULTS: Common cell remodeling patterns were observed across both diseases. Cell-cell communication analysis revealed that fibroblasts exhibited prominent outgoing and incoming signaling in both NSCLC and obese adipose tissues, predominantly through collagen, fibronectin, and CXCL12 pathways that target endothelial and immune cells. A total of 160 upregulated and 494 downregulated shared DEGs were identified; after stringent bulk RNA-seq validation, nine high-confidence candidates were retained, including CALCRL, NPR1, and TMEM100. These genes were enriched in endothelial differentiation, cell adhesion, and inflammatory signaling cascades.
DISCUSSION: The shared transcriptional features may point to a conserved stromal-vascular remodeling axis underlying the epidemiological link between obesity and NSCLC. The fibroblast-centered signaling patterns observed in both tissues suggest a common microenvironmental response, though functional studies are required to establish causality.
CONCLUSION: This dual scRNA-seq-based analysis suggests that fibroblasts may function as a conserved signaling hub and highlights 9 candidate genes and several FDA-approved agents warranting further functional validation for comorbidity management in obesity- associated NSCLC.

title: A staged combined parenteral and enteral nutritional support strategy in an elderly patient with non-small cell lung cancer, severe pneumonia, type II respiratory failure, and pre-existing malnutrition: a case report.
authors: Ding Q, Ding JR, Wang Q et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Severe respiratory critical illness with multiple comorbidities poses substantial challenges to nutritional management. Malnutrition is common but often underrecognized, and the optimal nutritional strategy remains unclear in patients with concurrent malignancy and prior gastrointestinal surgery. This case report describes the clinical application of a staged combined parenteral nutrition (PN) and enteral nutrition (EN) strategy in an elderly patient with complex multimorbidity, aiming to illustrate a practical, dynamically adjustable approach to nutritional support in similar settings.
CASE DESCRIPTION: A 79-year-old man with a history of gastric malignancy surgery was admitted with coma and dyspnea, and was diagnosed with non-small cell lung cancer, severe pneumonia, type II respiratory failure, and moderate malnutrition [body mass index (BMI) 16.9 kg/m2; Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 (NRS-2002) score 7; Subjective Global Assessment (SGA): moderate malnutrition]. A staged nutritional regimen combining PN and EN via a nasojejunal tube was implemented and dynamically adjusted over three phases based on his gastrointestinal tolerance and clinical evolution. During the intervention, white blood cell count (WBC) decreased from 22.90×109/L to 8.60×109/L and neutrophil percentage from 89.80% to 78.40%, indicating systemic inflammation control. Hemoglobin, total protein, and albumin initially improved but gradually declined with tumor progression. Oxygenation was maintained with peripheral oxygen saturation ≥98.4% under high-flow nasal oxygen after extubation.
CONCLUSIONS: This case illustrates that in elderly patients with critical respiratory illness complicated by malignancy, prior gastric surgery, and malnutrition, a staged PN-EN combined strategy can be implemented with dynamic adjustments based on tolerance and clinical changes. However, sustained nutritional improvement may be limited by persistent tumor catabolism and disease-related stress. Nutritional support should be closely coordinated with antitumor and anti-infective therapies. The findings are observational and derived from a single case, and further research is needed to confirm broader applicability.

title: AI-assisted 3D thoracic body composition analysis identifies candidate imaging markers associated with overall survival in older patients with lung cancer receiving radiotherapy.
authors: Sung S, Choi HJ, Jeong S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Older patients with lung cancer receiving thoracic radiotherapy have heterogeneous outcomes that are not fully captured by conventional clinical descriptors. We evaluated whether artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted three-dimensional (3D) thoracic body-composition analysis of pretreatment radiotherapy simulation computed tomography (CT) could identify candidate body-composition imaging markers associated with overall survival.
METHODS: This exploratory retrospective single-institution study included 88 patients aged 70 years or older who received thoracic radiotherapy for lung cancer between 2019 and 2021. Thoracic skeletal muscle and intermuscular fat were segmented using an AI-assisted workflow followed by expert review and Hounsfield unit-constrained refinement. Twelve knowledge-informed candidate groups were evaluated using conventional Cox regression. After marker selection, the selected marker pair was assessed in continuous form using bootstrap optimism correction, repeated five-fold cross-validation, and Uno's C-index. Penalized and alternative model-family analysis were performed as exploratory sensitivity analysis.
RESULTS: During follow-up, 28 deaths occurred. In an 18-case internal technical validation subset, the raw AI contours achieved Dice similarity coefficients of 0.930 for thoracic skeletal muscle and 0.723 for intermuscular fat. For Group 12, intermuscular adiposity index (IAI) and attenuation-weighted thoracic muscle fraction (TMF) were the variables that met the univariable screening criterion; the resulting two-marker model met the discrimination threshold without problematic collinearity. When modeled together, IAI values above the cohort median (hazard ratio [HR], 2.78; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.25-6.18; P = 0.012) and TMF values above the cohort median (HR, 3.77; 95% CI, 1.52-9.32; P = 0.004) were associated with poorer overall survival. In continuous form, the selected marker pair had an optimism-corrected Harrell's C-index of 0.751 (95% CI, 0.661-0.849), a mean repeated cross-validation C-index of 0.753 ± 0.112, and Uno's C-index of 0.737. These performance estimates were conditional on prior marker selection.
CONCLUSION: AI-assisted analysis of routine radiotherapy simulation CT identified IAI and TMF as candidate body-composition imaging markers associated with overall survival in this clinically heterogeneous cohort. The findings are exploratory and require independent evaluation in larger, clinically characterized cohorts before clinical use.

title: Multimodal digital assessment of early recovery after chest tube omission in early-stage lung cancer patients undergoing wedge resection: a post hoc analysis of a prospective cohort.
authors: Chen Y, Wang R, Li Y et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Given the limited surgical trauma associated with wedge resection, the clinical impact of routine chest tube drainage may be more apparent in early postoperative recovery than in safety outcomes alone. We used a multimodal digital platform integrating wearable monitoring and electronic patient-reported outcomes (ePROs) to compare recovery after wedge resection with and without chest tube placement.
METHODS: This study was a post hoc secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from a registered single-center observational cohort (NCT06118229). We included 98 patients from the parent cohort who had M0 primary lung cancer, underwent wedge resection, and had evaluable perioperative clinical and digital data; 54 were managed without chest tube placement and 44 with routine drainage. Propensity score matching yielded 34 matched pairs.
RESULTS: Compared with the chest tube group, the no chest tube group had a shorter postoperative hospital stay (2.51±1.11 vs. 3.14±1.03 days; P=0.02). Differences were most apparent in patient-reported recovery on postoperative day 2, with lower pain scores (2.79±2.11 vs. 4.08±2.07; P=0.03), less restless sleep (1.98±1.86 vs. 3.49±2.32; P=0.01), and less drowsiness (2.07±1.35 vs. 3.08±1.70; P=0.02). Wearable-derived physiologic trajectories were largely similar, although oxygen saturation on postoperative day 1 was higher in the no chest tube group (97.22%±1.64% vs. 96.05%±1.56%; P=0.003).
CONCLUSIONS: After wedge resection, omission of routine chest tube drainage was associated with a more favorable early patient-reported recovery, whereas physiologic differences were modest. Multimodal digital assessment may offer a practical and patient-centered approach to postoperative monitoring after minimally invasive thoracic surgery.

title: Sustained remission of NELL-1-positive membranous nephropathy after lung adenocarcinoma resection and during subsequent atezolizumab therapy in a 68-year-old man: a case report.
authors: Ikezawa M, Ikezawa Y, Eguchi M et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Membranous nephropathy (MN) is a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults and may occur secondary to malignancy, with lung cancer representing one of the most frequently associated malignancies. Neural epidermal growth factor-like 1 (NELL-1), identified as a target antigen in MN in 2019, has been associated with malignancy, although reported frequencies vary across cohorts. Clinical data regarding the course of NELL-1-positive MN during cancer recurrence and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) therapy remain limited.
CASE DESCRIPTION: A 68-year-old man with no significant past medical history, a 33-pack-year smoking history, and previous occupational concrete dust exposure presented with bilateral lower extremity edema. Laboratory testing revealed nephrotic syndrome [serum albumin: 1.3 g/dL, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR): 8.0 g/gCr, serum creatinine: 1.12 mg/dL]. Renal biopsy showed diffuse glomerular basement membrane (GBM) thickening with holes, subepithelial electron-dense deposits, relative immunoglobulin G (IgG) 1 predominance, and strong NELL-1 positivity, establishing NELL-1-positive MN. Subsequent malignancy screening identified a 15-mm pulmonary nodule, which was histopathologically diagnosed as stage IIIA (pT1bN2M0) lung adenocarcinoma following surgical resection. Without corticosteroids or immunosuppressive therapy, proteinuria declined after resection; at 4 months, serum albumin was 2.4 g/dL, UPCR 2.3 g/gCr, and serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. Renal parameters subsequently continued to improve, without nephrotic relapse. Eight months after surgery, multiple pulmonary metastases developed, and carboplatin, nab-paclitaxel, and atezolizumab were initiated. Before ICI initiation, renal remission had been established, with serum albumin of 3.6-3.8 g/dL, serum creatinine of approximately 1.1 mg/dL, and negative proteinuria. This remission was maintained throughout approximately 15 months of atezolizumab therapy, with persistently negative proteinuria, stable renal function, a sustained partial tumor response, and no nephrotic relapse. Immunohistochemical staining of the resected primary lung tumor showed no NELL-1 expression.
CONCLUSIONS: Resolution of nephrotic syndrome following tumor resection suggests a possible paraneoplastic relationship in this case of NELL-1-positive MN, despite absent NELL-1 expression in the primary tumor. Sustained renal remission during cancer recurrence and atezolizumab therapy suggests that ICI therapy may be feasible in selected patients with resolved paraneoplastic MN under close renal monitoring. This case highlights the importance of malignancy screening in patients with NELL-1-positive MN.

title: Hijacking Developmental Immunity: Inflammation and Immune Dysregulation in Pediatric Brain Tumors.
authors: Roy R, Kerl K
abstract: Pediatric brain tumors (PBTs) remain a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in children, underscoring the need for more effective therapeutic strategies. These tumors arise from disrupted neurodevelopmental programs and evolve within a developmentally constrained immune landscape that is tolerogenic, epigenetically plastic, and susceptible to tumor-mediated co-option. Increasing evidence indicates that, besides molecular heterogeneity, the tumor immune microenvironment critically influences clinical outcomes. Despite its therapeutic promise, immunotherapy has yet to demonstrate consistent clinical benefit in most PBTs, highlighting the need for rational multimodal strategies guided by deeper understanding of tumor-immune interactions in the developing brain. To provide a comprehensive perspective on fetal immune ontogeny and its tumor-driven dysregulation we used medulloblastoma, pediatric gliomas, atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors, and ependymoma as representative entities. Drawing on insights from developmental neurobiology, tumor immunology, and emerging multi-omic studies, we outline how PBTs exploit physiological immune maturation programs to establish immune evasion, sustain chronic inflammation, and promote therapy resistance. We further discuss emerging multimodal immunotherapeutic strategies and next-generation CAR T-cell approaches currently under clinical investigation. In addition, we highlight therapeutic avenues such as targeting tumor-associated myeloid populations and key inflammatory regulators that may offer promising opportunities for future clinical translation. We believe this Review will help address current limitations in preclinical models, improve patient stratification and guide rational design of therapeutic strategies.

title: A narrative review of barrier-matched engineering of macrophages for solid tumor immunotherapy: design logic, translational barriers and clinical outlook.
authors: Wu J, Dong J, Shen Y et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Macrophages are being investigated as adoptive cell therapies for solid tumors because they can migrate into tissues, phagocytose tumor cells, present antigen, secrete cytokines, and interact with stromal and other myeloid cells. However, their plasticity is also a liability. Once transferred into solid tumors, macrophages are exposed to hypoxia, metabolic stress, suppressive cytokines, and tumor-derived signals that may reduce phagocytosis, dampen inflammatory activation, and redirect them toward tumor-associated macrophage (TAM)-like, tumor-supportive phenotypes. This review examines engineered macrophage therapy through a barrier-matched framework.
METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and ClinicalTrials.gov were initially searched from database inception to 24 December 2024, with a supplementary search update conducted through 21 July 2026. Search terms covered engineered macrophages, chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-M), solid tumors, the tumor microenvironment, phagocytosis checkpoints, macrophage backpacks, nanoparticle macrophages, and stem-cell-derived macrophages. Peer-reviewed original studies, clinical trial reports, high-quality reviews, and registered trials directly relevant to macrophage- or myeloid-cell-based cancer immunotherapy were selected. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis was performed.
KEY CONTENT AND FINDINGS: Solid tumors impose five interacting barrier layers on macrophage therapy: physical barriers, metabolic barriers, immunosuppressive barriers, anti-phagocytic barriers, and phenotypic-plasticity barriers. These include restricted infiltration through dense extracellular matrix and abnormal vasculature, hypoxia, lactate accumulation, extracellular adenosine (eAdo)-A2A receptor (A2AR) signaling, suppressive tumor microenvironmental cues, do-not-eat-me checkpoints such as CD47-SIRPα, and TAM-like reprogramming after transfer. Engineering strategies have therefore shifted from simple cell transfer toward barrier-matched design. Some approaches add tumor-directed recognition, as in CAR-M or ligand-modified macrophages. Others aim to preserve inflammatory or phagocytic activity, deliver local payloads, attenuate inhibitory signaling, define scalable cell sources, or improve release and safety testing. The evidence base remains uneven. CAR-M has entered early clinical testing, whereas many nanoparticle-armed, backpack-based, stimulus-responsive, and genome-edited systems remain largely preclinical.
CONCLUSIONS: Engineered macrophage therapy should be guided by the dominant barrier layer in a given solid tumor setting rather than by the number of modifications added to the cell product. Future development requires clearer links between engineering modules, barrier-adapted translational readouts, manufacturing feasibility, persistence, safety, and rational trial design.

title: Brain-iT Immunotherapy: The Neurotransmitters Dopamine, Glutamate, GnRH-II and Neuropeptide Y Revive, Activate and Empower Healthy T Cells, Exhausted T Cells of Cancer Patients, and Genetically Engineered CAR T Cells.
authors: Levite M
abstract: Neurotransmitters are critical signaling molecules of the nervous system that activate their receptors within milliseconds, and convey accurate, coordinated, tightly regulated and important messages from one nerve cell, across a synapse, to another nerve, muscle or gland cell. It is time to realize that specific neurotransmitters also activate T cells directly and rapidly via their receptors in T cells. Subsequently, they decrease immune checkpoint inhibitors, increase expression of critical receptors, and induce a kaleidoscope of effector T cell functions. This review summarizes our discoveries of direct, activating, rejuvenating, and strengthening effects of either Dopamine, Glutamate, GnRH-II or Neuropeptide Y, or their combinations on human T cells of five origins: (1) normal T cells of healthy people, (2) exhausted T cells of head and neck cancer patients, (3) exhausted T cells of hepatocellular carcinoma patients, (4) exhausted T cells of glioblastoma patients, and (5) human genetically-engineered CAR T cells. The beneficial effects of these neurotransmitters on healthy T cells and on exhausted T cells of cancer patients include the following: depolarization; simultaneous decreased expression of key checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1, LAG-3, Tim-3, TIGIT and CD160); increased expression of CD3 zeta chain, CD147/EMM-PRIN/Basigin and 67kDa laminin receptor; and increased adhesion to fibronectin and laminin, chemotactic migration to SDF-1, migration toward autologous tumors, gene expression, cytokine secretion, proliferation, and arrest of human cancer cells. The direct effects of GnRH-II, Dopamine, or Glutamate on human anti-breast cancer ErbB-2+ CAR T cells were discovered in a yet unpublished collaborative research with Professor Zelig Eshhar, the pioneering scientist who invented and developed the concept of T-bodies, later re-named CAR T cells. The direct effects of the neurotransmitters on these CAR T cells include (1) dramatically increased expression of: CD3 zeta, CD147 and CXCR4, within only 30 minutes; (2) increased chemotactic migration towards SDF-1; (3) increased migration toward breast cancer cells; (4) increased penetration of the bone marrow of SCID mice; (5) increased homing to human breast cancer in SCID mice; and (6) increased inhibition of human breast cancer in SCID mice. In summary, either Glutamate, Dopamine, Neuropeptide Y, GnRH-II or their combinations, can activate, rescue, and strengthen healthy, exhausted, and genetically engineered CAR T cells. A novel personalized adoptive immunotherapy, called Brain-iT Immunotherapy, was invented and patented, and the review details its diagnostic and therapeutic stages for either patient's exhausted T cells or genetically engineered CAR T cells.

title: Review Article: Overcoming Antigen Expression Barriers in CAR-T Therapy for Solid Tumors.
authors: Moon OR, Bridgeman JS, Bao L
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy has transformed the treatment landscape for hematologic malignancies, achieving deep and durable responses across multiple FDA approved products. This progress stems from foundational discoveries initiated by Zelig Eshhar, whose early demonstrations that T cells could be redirected using synthetic receptors laid the conceptual groundwork for modern CAR-T design. Despite these successes, translating CAR-T therapy into solid cancers remains challenging. Solid tumors present unique obstacles including antigen heterogeneity, immunosuppressive microenvironments, limited T cell trafficking, and multiple mechanisms of antigen escape. Case studies across key solid tumor targets such as mesothelin, interleukin 13 receptor alpha 2 (IL13Rα2), claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2), glypican 3 (GPC3), epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2), and ganglioside D2 (GD2) highlight both the promise of CAR-T therapy and the biological complexities that limit durable clinical benefit. To address these barriers, next generation engineering strategies incorporating multispecific targeting, adaptor platforms, and logic gated receptor circuits (OR, AND, NOT, and multi-layered designs) are being developed to enhance tumor specificity, mitigate on-target/off-tumor toxicity, and prevent antigen escape. Armored CAR-T cells capable of overcoming suppressive tumor microenvironments further expand therapeutic potential. Collectively, these advances signal a shift from single antigen targeting to programmable, modular T cell therapies capable of responding to the multifaceted challenges of solid tumors. As the field integrates synthetic biology innovations with lessons learned from decades of clinical practice, CAR-T therapy is poised for broader applicability across both hematologic and solid cancers, extending the legacy of Eshhar's pioneering work.

title: Review Article: The Extracellular Matrix as a Barrier for CAR-T Cell Therapy in Solid Tumors.
authors: Revach OY
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapies, based on introducing a genetically modified T cell receptor to a patient's T cells, have transformed the treatment of hematological tumors. However, their efficacy in solid tumors is limited to date. Among the multiple barriers that shape CAR-T cell efficacy, including antigen heterogeneity, hypoxic tumor microenvironment (TME), and immunosuppressive cell populations, the altered extracellular matrix (ECM) has emerged as a dominant but understudied obstacle. In this review, we summarize the key ECM alterations characteristic of solid tumors and highlight the physical and molecular features that limit CAR-T cell function and promote exhaustion. We further discuss strategies to overcome these constraints and therapy resistance, as well as approaches to assess CAR-T therapy efficacy in clinically relevant models.

title: Review Article: Does CAR-T Cell Therapy of Solid Cancer Need the Activation of an Innate Immune Response?
authors: Barden M, Harrer C, Abken H
abstract: CAR-T cells have shown efficacious in the treatment of hematologic malignancies; however, their efficacy towards solid tumors is so far limited by multiple challenges such as poor T cell infiltration, limited persistence, and immune suppression within the tumor tissue. On the other hand, tumor regression, especially of metastases, can spontaneously occur, which has long intrigued the scientific community. Spontaneous regression is thought to be associated with a more global immune response, triggered through the activation of both innate and adaptive immune cells. The viewpoint discusses strategies for combining CAR-T cell therapy with approaches stimulating innate immune responses to facilitate clearance of solid tumors. Currently explored approaches include vaccination, cytokine-driven activation, contact-dependent immune cell interactions, and pharmacological co-treatment, all aiming at reshaping the local environment through recruiting and activating innate immune cells together with CAR-T cells to form a more comprehensive anti-tumor response.

title: Review Article: The Evolution and Future of Immunotherapy: The Promise of CAR T Cell-Derived Extracellular Vesicles.
authors: Aharon A, Levin AG
abstract: CAR T cell therapy, pioneered by Prof. Zelig Eshhar, has transformed hematologic malignancies but faces significant barriers in solid tumors, including poor infiltration, toxicity, and cytokine release syndrome. This perspective explores CAR T cell-derived extracellular vesicles (CAR T EVs) as an emerging platform that extends Eshhar's vision by delivering CAR-mediated cytotoxicity with enhanced tumor penetration, physiological barrier, and reduced immunogenicity. EVs carry functional CARs as immunomodulatory cargo, enabling precise antigen targeting without cellular proliferation risks. Key advantages and challenges are reviewed. Building on Eshhar's foundational work, CAR T EVs represent a nanotechnology-immunotherapy alternative.

title: In vivo engineering of CAR natural killer cells for immunotherapy using ligand-directed lipid nanoparticles.
authors: Chen Y, Monkovic J, Mughal H et al.
abstract: Targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) offer a nonviral approach for in vivo cell engineering but efficient programming of natural killer (NK) cells remains underexplored. Here we develop NK cell-targeted LNPs (NtLNPs) using engineered biparatopic NK cell ligands to drive receptor-specific uptake and mRNA delivery. Lead NtLNPs achieve up to ~80% NK cell transfection with minimal off-target effects in mice. Systemic delivery of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) mRNA using NtLNPs generates CAR NK cells in vivo. CD19-targeted CAR NKs completely deplete circulating B cells in healthy mice and CD3-targeted CAR NKs eliminate nearly all autoreactive T cells in an autoimmune hepatitis model, highlighting a potential advantage over CAR T therapies for T cell-driven disease. In solid tumors, NtLNPs targeting the inhibitory checkpoint NKG2A enhance antitumor efficacy by relieving Qa-1b-mediated immunosuppression. Lastly, we optimized NtLNPs for in vivo engineering of human CAR NK cells, enabling regression of two humanized hematologic malignancy models and establishing NtLNPs as a modular immunotherapy system.

title: CRISPRa screen unveils noncanonical NF-κB to boost the antitumor activity of TCR-based CAR-T cells.
authors: Yu H, Wu Y, Liu Y et al.
abstract: Engineering autologous T cells for adoptive therapies has revolutionized cancer treatment, yet limited persistence remains a major barrier to robust clinical responses and durable disease control. Although costimulation with 4-1BB markedly improves CAR-T-cell persistence, no comparably effective approach has been identified to enhance persistence in T-cell therapies that rely on native TCR signaling, including conventional TCR-T cells and synthetic T-cell receptor and antigen receptor (STAR) T cells. To identify intrinsic persistence regulators in a TCR-based context, we performed an in vivo CRISPR activation screen in STAR-T cells and identified the noncanonical NF-κB axis, with RELB as the top hit. Direct RELB overexpression, however, exhibited dose-dependent cytotoxicity, motivating a translational alternative: overexpression of p52, the ncNF-κB transcription partner of RELB. Under prolonged antigen exposure, p52 overexpression sustained proliferation, preserved effector functions, and increased the intratumoral trafficking potential, particularly in CD8⁺ T cells, thereby yielding superior tumor control. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling revealed coordinated upregulation of cell cycle programs and chemokine receptors, along with downregulation of apoptosis and exhaustion-associated modules. Moreover, p52 overexpression restored RELB nuclear translocation in the context of PD-1/PD-L1 engagement, indicating partial resistance to checkpoint-mediated suppression and sustained ncNF-κB activity in PD-L1hi immunosuppressive environments. Collectively, our findings identify p52 as an antigen-dependent enhancer of ncNF-κB, conferring durable persistence and checkpoint resilience on TCR-based T cells and providing a feasible strategy to improve therapeutic effects in solid tumors.

title: Affinity-optimized bispecific CAR-T cells targeting HLA-G and CD70 for the treatment of clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
authors: Su L, Ma X, Chen D et al.

title: Targeting CCR1/CCR2 attenuates cytokine release syndrome while preserving CAR T-cell antitumor activity.
authors: Li YR, Chen Y, Zhu Y et al.
abstract: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a major dose-limiting toxicity of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, yet the upstream mechanisms driving macrophage activation remain incompletely understood. Here, we established a xenograft model of human CAR T-cell therapy that recapitulates key features of CRS and combined single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with pharmacological intervention to define the inflammatory programs underlying CRS. CAR T-cell treatment induced dose-dependent systemic inflammation and remodeled the host myeloid compartment, leading to the accumulation of a distinct population of CRS-associated macrophages. Analysis of clinical scRNA-seq datasets from CAR T cell-treated glioblastoma patients confirmed enrichment of the CRS-associated macrophage gene signature following therapy in patients, supporting the clinical relevance of our findings. Transcriptomic analyses identified marked upregulation of the chemokine receptors CCR1 and CCR2 together with activation of CCL3- and CCL2-associated signaling pathways. Pharmacological inhibition of CCR1 and CCR2 significantly reduced clinical CRS, inflammatory cytokine production, and macrophage activation while preserving CAR T-cell expansion, effector cytokine production, and in vivo antitumor efficacy. These findings identify CCR1/CCR2-dependent chemokine signaling as a critical regulator of macrophage-driven CRS and support chemokine receptor blockade as a promising strategy to improve the safety of CAR T-cell therapy without compromising therapeutic efficacy.

title: Locoregionally delivered PD-1 blockade augments B7-H3 targeting CAR T cell efficacy in models of glioblastoma.
authors: Khan JF, Abrahimi P, Cai W et al.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a lethal brain tumor with a 95% five-year mortality rate, and remains a major unmet clinical need. An innovative approach to target GBM is administration of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells. In this study we identified B7-H3 as a favorable target antigen for CAR T cell therapy of GBM and developed a B7-H3 targeting CAR T cell. This CAR demonstrates robust, antigen-specific cytolysis and cytokine production, low tonic signaling, and preservation of a stem/naïve cell phenotype. Using orthotopic xenograft models of GBM we show that a single intravenous administration of this B7-H3 targeted CAR confers tumor control, and long-term survival. We identified upregulation of T cell inhibitory ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2 as a mechanism of resistance, and modified our B7-H3 targeting CAR vector to include a secreted a PD-1 blocking scFv. We further demonstrate that concomitant PD-1 blockade by the secreted PD-1 blocking scFv augments the antitumor capabilities of B7-H3-targeting CAR T cells through increased intratumoral infiltration by the CAR T cells and improved effector function. These data demonstrate B7-H3 targeting CAR T cells with concomitant PD-1 blockade is a safe and efficient method for improving the antitumor capacity of CAR T cells for GBM.

title: Tris-CAR-T Cell Therapy Targeting CD44 and CD133 in Newly Diagnosed Glioblastoma
summary:
This is an investigator-initiated, randomized, open-label, parallel-controlled clinical study designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of locally administered Tris-CAR-T cells in adults with newly diagnosed glioblastoma.

A total of 60 postoperative participants with IDH-wildtype WHO CNS grade 4 glioblastoma will be randomized 1:1 to the experimental group or the control group, with 30 participants in each group.

Participants in the experimental group will receive Ommaya reservoir implantation followed by local intratumoral or intraventricular Tris-CAR-T cell injections, and then standard temozolomide-based chemoradiotherapy and adjuvant temozolomide. If tumor progression occurs during Tris-CAR-T cell therapy, Tris-CAR-T treatment will be discontinued, and participants will transition to standard temozolomide-based chemoradiotherapy.

Participants in the control group will receive standard temozolomide-based chemoradiotherapy and adjuvant temozolomide.

The primary objective is to evaluate progression-free survival. Secondary objectives include overall survival, 12-month objective response rate, 12-month disease control rate, and safety.

title: Co-targeting KRAS and BCL-2 induces pyroptosis and antitumor tertiary lymphoid structures
summary: Mutant KRAS drives lung tumorigenesis through both cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic mechanisms, yet mutation subtype-specific differences in metabolic regulation and immune evasion remain incompletely understood. Here we show that the KRAS G12D mutation, particularly in the KRAS/STK11 co-mutant (KL) context, is associated with poor prognosis and a suppressed immune microenvironment characterized by impaired antigen presentation. At the cell-intrinsic level, G12D exhibits weakened interaction with hexokinase 1 (HK1), reduced spare respiratory capacity, and diminished mitochondrial stress resistance compared with G12C. Based on this mitochondrial vulnerability, we screened a panel of clinically available agents that induce mitochondrial stress and identified that co-targeting KRAS and BCL-2 synergistically triggers GSDME-mediated pyroptosis predominantly in G12D tumors. This combination further induces functional tertiary lymphoid structures (TLS) in vivo. Immune cell depletion experiments further demonstrate that the antitumor efficacy is dramatically dependent on B cells. Moreover, this treatment strategy induced membrane attack complex (MAC) deposition in situ and elicited memory antitumor responses. Collectively, these findings establish that combined KRAS and BCL-2 inhibition elicits pyroptosis and TLS formation, leading to B-cell-dependent in situ and memory antitumor immunity, providing a mechanistic rationale for targeting mitochondrial-immune crosstalk in KRAS G12D-mutant lung cancer.

title: Trp53 heterozygosity defines novel states impacting tumor plasticity and progression in Kras-initiated non-small cell lung cancer
summary: KRAS and TP53 are frequently mutated in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. The most common event at the TP53 locus is mutation/loss of one allele and retention of a wild-type allele, which confers better survival outcomes than complete TP53 loss. To study the contribution of TP53 heterozygosity, we generated a murine lung tumor model with a KrasG12D mutation and intact (K) or single-allele loss (KP+/-) of Trp53 and compared it with publicly available complete loss (KP) data. K and KP+/- mice lived longer than KP mice, paralleling clinical survival data. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of tumor-burdened lungs indicated that Trp53 heterozygosity expanded transcriptional plasticity that was not present in K and KP tumors. Genomic instability was also higher in KP+/- mice relative to the KP genotype. Trp53 gene dosage, thus, regulates phenotypic plasticity and evolutionary trajectories of tumor states across K, KP+/-, and KP tumors. Murine KP+/- tumor signatures and copy-number profiles were present in human NSCLC datasets. Two of these signatures correlated with better and worse patient survival outcomes, respectively. TP53 heterozygosity in KRAS-mutant lung cancers presents a distinct genomic landscape that should be taken into account in the development of novel therapeutic strategies.

title: LuTuFlow: a deep learning-based pipeline for quantitative characterization of mouse lung tumors in CT imaging
summary: Computed tomography (CT) is a widely used, non-invasive imaging tool to monitor tumor growth. Tumor identification and volumetric quantification are crucial for assessing tumor burden, whereas tracking individual tumors by aligning scans from multiple time points reveals disease progression. However, these processes remain largely dependent on manual analysis, limiting the accuracy, reproducibility, objectivity, and scalability of tumor characterization. Several deep learning models have enabled automated segmentation and object identification. However, open-source, integrated software platforms that cover the entire workflow - including processing raw CT images, annotating and tracking tumors through time, and generating data reports and visualizations - are still needed. Here, we present LuTuFlow, a computer vision pipeline incorporating a nnU-Net-based deep learning model, configured for murine lung segmentation and tumor analysis. We integrated these modules into a Napari plugin, allowing researchers to apply the entire automated workflow to transform raw CT scan datasets into quantitative readouts and interactive visualizations in a simple graphical user interface. The resulting model, iteratively refined using expert-corrected annotations, generated reliable quantitative estimates of tumor burden.

title: Second- and third-line outcomes after selective RET inhibitor failure in RET fusion-positive metastatic lung cancer: A real-world analysis from the RET-MAP registry.
authors: Miliziano D, Rotow JK, Lomibao M et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Selective RET inhibitors (SRIs) are the first-line standard for RET fusion-positive NSCLC, but no treatment is established after progression. Real-world outcomes are needed to inform trial design and contextualize single-arm studies in this rare population.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: Using the international RET-MAP registry (52 centers), we evaluated second-line platinum-pemetrexed with or without immunotherapy after first-line SRI progression and characterized third-line treatments after exposure to both regimens in any order.
RESULTS: Among 207 patients treated with first-line SRI, 81 (39%) discontinued because of progression; 65 (80%) received subsequent therapy, most commonly platinum-pemetrexed with or without immunotherapy (n=35, 54%). At 53 months' median follow-up, real-world objective response rate was 41% (12/29), median real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS) 6.1 months (95% CI 4.8-11.4), and median overall survival (OS) 13.7 months (95% CI 8.7-26.5). Outcomes were similar with chemotherapy alone (n=12) versus chemo-immunotherapy (n=23) for rwPFS (5.9 vs 6.8 months; HR 1.05, p=0.903) and OS (18.5 vs 13.7 months; HR 0.83, p=0.674). Three patients had rwPFS beyond 24 months with chemo-immunotherapy, all after short first-line SRI exposure. Among 32 patients receiving third-line therapy, taxane with or without antiangiogenic therapy was most common (n=11), with no responses and median rwPFS of 1.5 months (95% CI 0.8-NR).
CONCLUSIONS: Second-line platinum-pemetrexed with or without immunotherapy achieved a median rwPFS of 6.1 months. Third-line outcomes were poor, highlighting the need for new treatment strategies.

title: A plain language summary of the 7-year results from the CROWN study: lorlatinib compared with crizotinib in people with ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Shaw AT, Solomon BJ, Felip E et al.

title: Pralsetinib-induced interstitial pneumonitis in a patient with metastatic pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma harboring RET fusion: a case report.
authors: Zhang J, Huang J, Li X et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma (PSC), an exceptionally rare subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), remains poorly characterized in terms of molecular alterations, rendering targeted therapy a promising option. RET gene fusions act as oncogenic drivers across multiple tumor types, and the emergence of selective RET tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) like pralsetinib has transformed the treatment of RET-fusion positive malignancies. However, their expanding clinical use underscores the need to better understand adverse event (AE) profiles, particularly severe toxicities.
CASE DESCRIPTION: This report describes a 60-year-old male who presented with progressive hemoptysis. Bronchoscopic biopsy, combined with pathological evaluation, immunohistochemical staining, and next-generation sequencing (NGS), confirmed the diagnosis of metastatic PSC (favor spindle cell type, cT4N2M1a, stage IVa) harboring a KIF5B-RET fusion. The patient was initiated on pralsetinib, achieving a sustained partial response (PR) for 25 months. Subsequently, he developed pralsetinib-induced grade 3 interstitial pneumonitis, which resolved following immediate drug discontinuation and systemic glucocorticoid intervention. A pralsetinib rechallenge at a reduced dose was attempted but resulted in recurrent pneumonitis, mandating permanent treatment cessation. The patient's condition rapidly deteriorated, leading to his unfortunate demise.
CONCLUSIONS: Pralsetinib is effective for RET-fusion positive PSC, achieving long-term disease control. However, its risk of severe interstitial pneumonitis highlights the need for close monitoring. Clinicians should balance risks and benefits, especially for rechallenge, to optimize outcomes.

title: Impact of different TP53 mutation subtypes on response and outcome in advanced lung adenocarcinoma receiving first-line immunotherapy or chemo-immunotherapy.
authors: Quan X, Xuzhang W, Shen S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immunotherapy, either as a monotherapy or in combination with chemotherapy, has become the standard first-line treatment for advanced lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) without driver mutations. Although TP53 is frequently mutated in LUAD, the clinical significance of different TP53 mutation subtypes in the setting of first-line immunotherapy remains poorly defined. This study aimed to evaluate the association between TP53 mutation subtypes and treatment outcomes in patients with locally advanced or metastatic LUAD receiving first-line immunotherapy or chemo-immunotherapy.
METHODS: A total of 129 locally advanced or metastatic LUAD patients with TP53 mutations receiving first-line immunotherapy or chemo-immunotherapy between January 2018 and November 2022 at Shanghai Chest Hospital were retrospectively analyzed. TP53 mutation status was confirmed by next-generation sequencing (NGS). Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards model were employed to analyze the effect of TP53 mutation subtypes on treatment outcomes.
RESULTS: TP53 mutations were categorized into four groups: missense, nonsense, frameshift, and others. Missense mutations were the most frequent subtype (78/129, 60.5%), followed by frameshift (23/129, 17.8%), nonsense (18/129, 14.0%), and others (10/129, 7.8%). Patients with TP53 frameshift mutations exhibited worse progression-free survival (PFS) (median PFS, 6.0 vs. 13.5 months; P=0.002) and overall survival (OS) (median OS, 13.3 vs. 39.9 months; P<0.001) than those with non-frameshift mutations. A significantly higher proportion of patients in the frameshift group experienced progressive disease (PD) as their best overall response than in the non-frameshift group (30.4% vs. 7.6%, P=0.006). In multivariate analysis, TP53 frameshift mutations remained independently associated with inferior PFS [hazard ratio (HR) =2.229, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.337-3.715, P=0.002] and OS (HR =3.278, 95% CI: 1.730-6.210, P<0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective cohort, TP53 frameshift mutations were associated with poorer survival in patients with advanced LUAD receiving first-line immunotherapy or chemo-immunotherapy, suggesting distinct prognostic implications across TP53 mutation subtypes.

title: Efficacy and safety of adjuvant ensartinib in stage I ALK-positive NSCLC patients: a retrospective, multicenter study.
authors: Gao Z, Zheng J, Jia L et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The role of adjuvant ensartinib in patients with stage I ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with high-risk pathological features remains unclear. This multicenter retrospective study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of adjuvant ensartinib in this population.
METHODS: A total of 393 patients with completely resected stage I ALK-positive NSCLC were included from five centers in China between March 2017 and March 2026. Patients were categorized into the ensartinib group (n = 63) and the observation group (n = 330). Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and propensity score matching (PSM) were employed to balance baseline characteristics. The primary endpoint was disease-free survival (DFS). Secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS) and safety.
RESULTS: After IPTW, baseline characteristics were well balanced between groups. The ensartinib group showed a higher 3-year DFS rate compared with the observation group (100% vs. 90.2%;P = 0.014). In patients with high-risk pathological features (micropapillary or solid subtypes or complex glandular pathological subtypes ≥10%, mucinous adenocarcinoma, or spread through air spaces), the 3-year DFS was 100% in the ensartinib group versus 86.5% in the observation group (P = 0.016). No significant difference in OS was observed between groups. Adverse events occurred in 87.3% of patients in the ensartinib group, all of which were grade 1-2, with rash being the most common adverse event (85.7%).
CONCLUSION: Exploratory analyses suggested an association between adjuvant ensartinib and favorable DFS outcomes in stage I ALK-positive NSCLC patients exhibiting high-risk pathological features. A favorable safety profile was also observed. For patients without high-risk factors, the benefit of adjuvant ensartinib remains to be further clarified. These findings are hypothesis-generating and support further prospective evaluation of risk-adapted adjuvant ALK-TKI therapy in stage I ALK-positive NSCLC.

title: Allostatic load, genetic susceptibility, and lung cancer risk: Evidence from a prospective cohort and integrative proteomic analyses.
authors: Yang F, Wang W, Chen F et al.
abstract: Allostatic load (AL), a composite measure of multisystem dysregulation associated with chronic stress, has been linked to lung cancer risk. However, its joint effects with genetic susceptibility and the biological pathways underlying this relationship remain unclear. We conducted a prospective cohort study of 336,945 UK Biobank participants to assess associations between AL and lung cancer incidence and its histological subtypes. A polygenic risk score was constructed to evaluate the joint associations of AL and genetic susceptibility. We further assessed whether AL provided incremental risk stratification beyond established low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening eligibility frameworks and integrated plasma proteomic data using machine learning, enrichment, and mediation analyses. We found that higher AL was associated with an increased risk of lung cancer (per-unit HR = 1.073, 95% CI: 1.053-1.094; Low vs. Normal HR = 1.284, 95% CI: 1.065-1.547; High vs. Normal HR = 1.629, 95% CI: 1.347-1.971). Subtype analyses revealed the strongest effect for small-cell lung cancer (SCLC), with significant associations also observed for lung adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma. High AL combined with high genetic risk was associated with a 136.9% increased risk (HR = 2.369, 95% CI: 1.565-3.583), without evidence of interaction. AL provided additional risk discrimination beyond established LDCT screening eligibility criteria. Proteomic analyses identified 111 AL-associated proteins and 34 proteins with potential mediation signal, including HGF, RARRES2, and GDF15, implicating inflammatory, metabolic, and growth factor-related processes as biological correlates of the AL-lung cancer association. In conclusion, higher AL was independently associated with lung cancer risk, particularly SCLC. Integrative proteomic analyses provided exploratory evidence for biological pathways that may link cumulative physiological dysregulation to lung carcinogenesis. Incorporating AL, as a composite biomarker reflecting cumulative physiological burden, into risk models may improve risk stratification and help identify individuals at elevated risk.

title: Endobronchial Pulmonary Typical Carcinoid Tumors in Young Adults: A Three-Case Series Highlighting Obstructive Complications and Surgical Outcomes.
authors: Alkhayer I, Aldakak MA, Abbas Y
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Typical pulmonary carcinoid tumors are uncommon, well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasms that often arise in the central airways and may present with nonspecific obstruction-related respiratory symptoms, resulting in delayed diagnosis. We report a three-case series of endobronchial typical pulmonary carcinoid tumors in young adults, highlighting their variable obstructive complications and surgical outcomes.
METHODS: This retrospective case series included three consecutive patients managed at a tertiary university hospital in Syria. Clinical presentation, imaging, bronchoscopic findings, operative details, histopathology, and follow-up data were obtained from medical records. All patients had histopathologically confirmed typical pulmonary carcinoid tumors with central/endobronchial involvement and underwent definitive surgical resection. Patient identifiers were removed, and written informed consent for publication and use of accompanying images was obtained.
RESULTS: The patients were 23-35 years old and presented with different manifestations of central airway obstruction: chronic productive cough (Case 1), post-obstructive suppuration with lung abscesses (Case 2), and recurrent hemoptysis with atelectatic/post-obstructive changes (Case 3). Bronchoscopy demonstrated obstructing endobronchial lesions in all three cases, and histopathology confirmed typical carcinoid tumors with low mitotic activity and no necrosis. Case 1 underwent right middle and lower bilobectomy with systematic mediastinal lymph node dissection for a large tumor staged T4N1M0. Cases 2 and 3 underwent left lower lobectomy; in Case 3, this included bronchial segment resection with primary closure and mediastinal lymph node dissection. Resection margins were negative in all cases, and mediastinal nodes were negative in Cases 2 and 3. No adjuvant therapy was administered. Follow-up showed no recurrence approximately 4.5 years after surgery in Case 1, clinical stability at one month in Case 2, and stable chest imaging at six months in Case 3.
CONCLUSION: Endobronchial typical pulmonary carcinoid tumors in young adults can produce diverse obstruction-related complications, including chronic cough, post-obstructive suppuration, and hemoptysis with atelectatic changes. Timely airway evaluation and complete surgical resection with appropriate nodal assessment can achieve favorable outcomes, including in locally advanced disease when complete resection is feasible.

title: Interpretable deep learning and radiomics for predicting the occurrence of brain metastases following prophylactic brain irradiation in small cell lung cancer.
authors: Zhang X, Zhao L, Wang J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Brain metastasis remains an important clinical concern in patients with small cell lung cancer (SCLC), even after prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI). Accurate identification of patients at high risk of brain metastasis after PCI may facilitate individualized surveillance and management. This study developed a fusion model based on two-and-a-half-dimensional (2.5D) multi-channel deep learning features, clinical features, and radiomics features to predict whether patients with SCLC will develop brain metastases following PCI.
METHODS: This retrospective study included 185 patients with SCLC who underwent PCI and randomly divided them into a training set (N=148) and a testing set (N=37). A 2.5D multi-channel convolutional neural network (CNN) model was constructed based on multi-planar regions of interest (ROI) derived from CT images to extract 2.5D deep learning features. Based on the largest cross-section and three-dimensional (3D) volume of the tumor ROI, two-dimensional (2D) and 3D deep learning features were extracted, respectively. Subsequently, features from different dimensions were fused with clinical features and traditional omics features to construct the 2D_clinic_Rad, 2.5D_clinic_Rad, and 3D_clinic_Rad models, respectively. The performance differences between the 3D models and the clinical and traditional radiomics models were then compared.
RESULTS: The 2.5D_clinic_Rad fusion model demonstrated the best performance in predicting brain metastases, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.841 on the test set, outperforming clinical models, traditional radiomics models, and 2D and 3D deep learning fusion models. Analysis of decision curves and calibration curves indicated that the 2.5D_clinic_Rad model demonstrated the highest clinical net benefit and the best calibration consistency compared to other models.
CONCLUSIONS: The fusion model based on 2.5D_clinic_Rad can effectively predict the risk of brain metastasis in patients with SCLC following whole-brain prophylactic irradiation.

title: Association of baseline hormone levels with outcomes of first-line immunotherapy in extensive-stage small cell lung cancer.
authors: Wang S, Meng R, Liu J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Endocrine dysregulation may influence immune function and clinical outcomes in cancer. This study investigated the prognostic relevance of baseline endocrine hormones in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC) receiving first-line immunotherapy.
METHODS: This retrospective multicenter cohort study included patients with ES-SCLC treated at multiple centers between January 2020 and December 2024. Baseline serum levels of cortisol, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), free triiodothyronine (FT3), free thyroxine (FT4), and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) were measured before treatment. Patients were stratified into high and low groups for each hormone based on median values. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards models.
RESULTS: A total of 377 patients were included, with a median PFS of 9.7 months and median OS of 16.7 months. Patients with high baseline cortisol had significantly shorter PFS (8.9 vs. 11.7 months, P=0.02) and OS (15.2 vs. 26.0 months, P=0.003). Elevated cortisol remained independently associated with inferior survival after multivariable adjustment [hazard ratio (HR) =1.540, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.04-2.15, P=0.03]. In contrast, baseline ACTH, FT3, FT4, and TSH were not significantly associated with PFS or OS.
CONCLUSIONS: Baseline cortisol is independently associated with survival outcomes in ES-SCLC patients receiving immunotherapy and may serve as a prognostic biomarker. These findings highlight the relevance of neuroendocrine-immune interactions and warrant prospective validation.

title: Development and external validation of an XGBoost-based prognostic model for small cell lung cancer with brain metastases.
authors: Jiao P, Chen C, Zhang K et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and brain metastases (BM) have poor and heterogeneous survival outcomes, while existing prognostic tools have shown limited discriminatory performance. We aimed to develop an extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) based prognostic model and perform preliminary external validation.
METHODS: Patients with small cell lung cancer and brain metastases (SCLCBM) diagnosed between 2010 and 2020 were identified from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database for model development and internal testing. External validation was performed in an independent single-center Chinese cohort. Variables screened by univariable Cox regression and retained in multivariable Cox regression analyses were used as predictors in the XGBoost models. Grid search was used for hyperparameter tuning, and candidate parameter combinations were evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. Model performance was assessed using the areas under the curves (AUCs) and confusion matrices, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was used to interpret model predictions.
RESULTS: The study included 7,692 patients from the SEER database and 128 patients in the external validation cohort. The final models incorporated demographic, tumor-related, treatment-related, and metastatic factors, including age, sex, T and N stages, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery, and extracranial metastases. AUCs for 3-, 6-, 12-, and 18-month overall survival (OS) were 0.840, 0.801, 0.738, and 0.759 in the internal testing cohort and 0.779, 0.790, 0.739, and 0.763 in the external cohort, respectively. SHAP analysis consistently ranked chemotherapy as the most influential predictor.
CONCLUSIONS: The XGBoost models showed moderate discrimination across the evaluated prediction horizons in both the internal testing cohort and a small single-center external cohort. Further validation in larger, prospective, multicenter cohorts is required before clinical use.
