title: Neuroendocrine prostate cancer converges on a fetal pulmonary neuroendocrine-like program.
authors: Yue W, Kyprianou N, Tewari AK et al.
abstract: Advanced prostate cancers can relapse as neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC), a treatment-resistant state that is independent of androgen receptor (AR) signaling and whose developmental identity remains unclear. We integrated single-cell, bulk, cistrome and spatial datasets across published cohorts and mapped malignant tumor states to human fetal atlases. In the discovery cohort (35,696 tumor cells, 20 patients), NEPC cells were malignant and shared copy-number architecture with adenocarcinoma (chromosome-level r = 0.64). NEPC most closely matched a fetal, lineage-restricted neuroendocrine program, best supported as pulmonary neuroendocrine-like among the alternatives tested (islet, chromaffin and sympathoblast), with the same direction across three cohorts; the pulmonary-versus-islet distinction was method-sensitive and remains provisional. Cross-sectional stage ordering and one illustrative single-tumor pseudotime analysis were consistent with luminal-program loss and neuroendocrine-program gain, while the specific ordering of individual transcription factors remained partly dataset-dependent. A regulatory screen using five methods nominated a circuit centered on ASCL1 whose convergent enhancers overlapped fetal pulmonary neuroendocrine chromatin and showed FOXA1 binding in cell-line and xenograft models (87.0% versus 33.8%; P = 0.016). In one NEPC Visium section, the program localized to malignant NEPC territory defined by copy number, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.85. Based on three NEPC patients with cross-cohort replication of direction, these data support NEPC as an adenocarcinoma-related malignant state converging on a fetal pulmonary neuroendocrine-like reference program and nominate regulatory and surface targets linked to ASCL1 for functional study.

title: Real-World Experience With Multimodal Treatment of Resectable Stage II-III Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Single Institutional Analysis.
authors: Griffo R, Niedermaier B, Klotz LV et al.
abstract: Neoadjuvant therapy has recently become an integral component of multimodal treatment for resectable lung cancer. However, real-world data on perioperative morbidity and treatment adherence remain limited. This study aimed to assess the feasibility and safety of different neoadjuvant treatment approaches applied within daily clinical routine. We retrospectively analyzed patients with resectable stage II-III non-small cell lung cancer undergoing either neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy or chemotherapy/chemoradiotherapy followed by curative surgical resection. Treatment groups were compared with respect to perioperative outcomes, radiologic and pathologic downstaging, and pathologic response. A total of 143 patients met the inclusion criteria, of whom 46 (32.2%) received chemoimmunotherapy and 97 (67.8%) were treated with chemotherapy prior to surgery. Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation occurred in only two patients in the chemoimmunotherapy group and four patients in the chemotherapy group. Chemoimmunotherapy was associated with significantly higher rates of pathologic complete response (37.0% vs. 4.1%) and more pronounced nodal downstaging, with a higher proportion of patients achieving ypN0 status (76.1% vs. 34.0%). High tumoral PD-L1 expression (≥ 50%) and squamous cell carcinoma histology were independently associated with pathologic complete response. Real-world treatment with neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy was feasible and resulted in improved response rates compared with chemotherapy, without increasing perioperative morbidity. Histology and high PD-L1 expression may serve as predictors for complete pathologic response, although the predictive value of PD-L1 requires confirmation in larger cohorts with more complete biomarker data.

title: Case Report: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced hypophysitis presenting as acute paralytic ileus mimicking mechanical bowel obstruction in a patient affected by advanced non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Baggi A, Adriani A, Ammoni LC et al.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have significantly improved outcomes in advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) but may induce immune-related adverse events (irAEs), including hypophysitis. Although endocrine irAEs usually present with nonspecific constitutional symptoms, atypical manifestations may delay diagnosis and expose patients to unnecessary invasive procedures. We report the case of a 76-year-old man with metastatic NSCLC receiving first-line nivolumab, ipilimumab, carboplatin, and pemetrexed who developed profound asthenia, altered mental status, bilious vomiting, and severe gastrointestinal dilation suggestive of acute mechanical bowel obstruction after two treatment cycles. Computed tomography demonstrated marked gastric and intestinal distension, and surgical management was initially considered. Endocrine evaluation subsequently revealed central hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency, consistent with ICI-induced hypophysitis. Prompt initiation of physiological hormone replacement with intravenous hydrocortisone followed by thyroid hormone supplementation resulted in rapid neurological and systemic recovery, complete restoration of gastrointestinal motility, radiological resolution of bowel dilatation, and avoidance of surgery. Follow-up imaging also demonstrated a partial tumor response, which has remained durable for more than two years without additional anticancer treatment while the patient continues long-term endocrine replacement therapy. This case expands the clinical spectrum of ICI-induced hypophysitis by describing an unusual presentation as acute paralytic ileus mimicking mechanical bowel obstruction. It underscores the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for endocrine irAEs in patients receiving ICIs who develop unexplained multisystem deterioration or apparent surgical abdomen. Early hormonal assessment and timely replacement therapy can be lifesaving, prevent unnecessary surgical interventions, and allow optimal multidisciplinary management without compromising oncologic outcomes.

title: Prognostic impact of immune-related adverse events in non-completers of durvalumab consolidation therapy for non-small cell lung cancer: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
authors: Ebi N, Kawabata R, Fujimoto M et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Durvalumab consolidation therapy after chemoradiotherapy (CRT) is standard for unresectable, locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, long-term outcomes, treatment discontinuation impact, and the prognostic significance of immune-related adverse events (irAEs)-controlling for immortal time bias-remain unclear. We evaluated overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) by completion status and irAE occurrence in an exploratory single-center cohort.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 59 consecutive NSCLC patients receiving durvalumab post-CRT (median follow-up: 53.6 months). Completion was defined as 12 months of therapy (completers, n=25; non-completers, n=34). Survival was estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. Time-dependent Cox regression evaluated irAE onset to adjust for immortal time bias, with sensitivity analyses stratified by discontinuation reason. Event-free patients were censored at last follow-up.
RESULTS: Of 59 patients (median age: 70 years), 25 (42%) completed therapy, while 34 (58%) discontinued early (disease progression: n=16, adverse events: n=15, preference: n=3). During follow-up, 28 deaths [completers: 8/25 (32%); non-completers: 20/34 (59%)] and 36 progression events [completers: 9/25 (36%); non-completers: 27/34 (79%)] occurred. Completers achieved superior median OS (70.9 vs. 39.2 months; 5-year OS: 61% vs. 22%; P<0.01) and PFS (not reached vs. 7.9 months; 5-year PFS: 52% vs. 11%; P<0.001). Among non-completers (n=34, 20 deaths), time-dependent Cox analysis showed irAE onset reduced mortality risk [hazard ratio (HR) =0.384; 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.147-0.999; P=0.0498], yielding a higher 5-year OS rate (43% vs. 0%, P=0.03). Stratified sensitivity analysis indicated a consistent directional trend, though limited by event counts (HR =0.44; 95% CI: 0.11-1.72; P=0.24).
CONCLUSIONS: One-year durvalumab completion remains the primary clinical objective. In patients discontinuing early, irAE onset was associated with a potential prognostic signal after controlling for time-varying bias; however, these findings represent cautious, hypothesis-generating observations requiring prospective multi-center validation.

title: Plasma proteomic profiles associated with low-dose computed tomography findings and incident lung cancer: a prospective pilot study.
authors: Tikkanen A, Iivanainen S, Luukkainen MEK et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Plasma proteins may reflect tumor-host biology, but their relationships with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) findings and incident lung cancer remain uncertain. Although LDCT screening has improved survival, challenges remain in risk stratification and interpretation of screening findings. The aim of the present study was to investigate associations between plasma proteomic profiles, LDCT findings and incident lung cancer, and to explore their potential for lung cancer risk stratification.
METHODS: In this prospective study, baseline plasma proteomic profiles and LDCT radiographic findings (baseline and follow-up) were analyzed in 193 participants with significant smoking history. A targeted panel of 92 proteins was used to evaluate associations with LDCT classifications and incident lung cancer. Five participants with non-lung malignancies were excluded, leaving 188 participants, including six incident lung cancer cases. Exploratory prediction models for lung cancer were developed using machine learning approaches.
RESULTS: Individuals with positive LDCT findings showed overexpression of multiple plasma proteins compared with those with indeterminate or negative findings; participants who developed lung cancer also showed differential protein expression compared with participants without cancer. While individual protein odds ratio (OR) estimates were imprecise, a seven-protein machine learning model, consisting of TNFRSF9, FGF2, CCL20, CD4, MMP12, CXCL11, and CD40 demonstrated an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.915 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.829-1.000] in predicting lung cancer. Proteomic profiling revealed associations of lung cancer with pathways, such as TNFα and IL6-JAK-STAT3 signaling, commonly linked to early carcinogenic processes.
CONCLUSIONS: Plasma proteomic profiling may provide complementary, biologically informative signals alongside LDCT in lung cancer screening. By integrating circulating biomarkers with imaging, this approach enables investigation of early disease biology in a pre-diagnostic setting, providing insights into systemic alterations that may precede clinically apparent cancer. While these findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish the clinical utility of plasma proteomics in LDCT screening, these findings justify the need to evaluate this approach for additional risk stratification in LDCT lung cancer screening. Larger independent studies are required to determine whether plasma proteomics can improve risk stratification beyond LDCT and thereby reduce unnecessary follow-up examinations.

title: A novel three-CpG signature for lung adenocarcinoma diagnosis: integrating multi-omics, machine learning, and clinical validation.
authors: Liu Q, Shen M, Yan L et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. The identification of non-invasive biomarkers for early detection is critical to improving patient outcomes. Integrative analysis of DNA methylation and gene expression represents a promising approach for identifying cancer-specific diagnostic markers. This study aimed to identify and validate a LUAD-specific DNA methylation signature for the early detection of LUAD.
METHODS: An integrated analysis of DNA methylation data from the Illumina HumanMethylation450K array, including 455 tumor samples, 32 normal samples, and RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) LUAD cohort was performed. Differential methylation and expression were identified, and LUAD-specific markers were selected by excluding probes altered in 10 other cancer types. All combinations of five candidate cytosine-phosphate-guanine (CpG) sites (excluding single-site combinations) were constructed using four machine learning algorithms, generating 104 models. A stringent two-step filtering strategy required each model to achieve an area under the curve (AUC) >0.8, F1 score >0.8, and coefficient of variation (CV) <0.1 in at least four of the five validation datasets [including TCGA test set and four independent Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) cohorts] and required each CpG combination to be validated by all four algorithms. Candidate methylation markers were experimentally validated by MethyLight quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) in 97 paired LUAD and 14 benign lung lesion samples.
RESULTS: We identified 6,840 differentially methylated sites (DMSs) and 3,020 differentially expressed genes (DEGs). Integration of multi-omics data revealed 132 genes with correlated methylation-expression patterns. After filtering for LUAD specificity, 36 methylation markers were retained. A three-CpG eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model (cg00817598 in WNT3, cg13470063 in TIE1, and cg23094674 in PLEKHA6) was selected as the optimal classifier, achieving an AUC of 0.995 in TCGA test set and AUC values ranging from 0.864 to 0.986 across the four GEO datasets. The model demonstrated robust cancer-type specificity (AUC: 0.771 in distinguishing LUAD from 565 other cancer samples) and outperformed established markers RASSF1A and SHOX2 (average AUC: 0.725-0.937). Experimental validation confirmed significant hypermethylation of all three CpG sites in LUAD tissues (all P<0.001). The model achieved an AUC of 0.832 in distinguishing LUAD from benign lesions. Methylation levels of cg23094674 and cg00817598 showed positive correlations with tumor size and progressively increased from benign lesions to early-stage and advanced LUAD.
CONCLUSIONS: A three-CpG methylation signature was identified that may serve as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic biomarker for LUAD, supported by rigorous model selection, multi-dataset validation, and experimental confirmation. The ability of the signature to distinguish LUAD from other cancer types and benign lesions highlights its strong potential for clinical translation as a non-invasive assay for detection.

title: Abolition by design: implementing the dismantling of the commercial tobacco and nicotine industry.
authors: Maddox R, Kawenata Bradbrook S
abstract: The commercial tobacco and nicotine industry continues to drive preventable disease and death globally. Despite progress in tobacco control, industry power, product diversification, market expansion, and policy interference have constrained the impact of incremental regulatory approaches. Downstream interventions, such as cessation supports and lung cancer screening, remain essential but respond to accumulated harms rather than preventing exposure at its source. This paper presents an implementation framework that positions abolition as a staged, governable, and legally supported public health strategy. Rather than a symbolic endpoint, abolition is conceptualized as a sequenced governance process through which industry structures can be dismantled using existing regulatory, fiscal, and enforcement mechanisms. These mechanisms are embedded within national systems and international instruments, including the World Health Organization Framework Convention on Tobacco Control and international human rights instruments. Abolition is mischaracterized as consumer prohibition. This reflects a category error that evaluates abolition using prohibition logics, obscuring its focus on dismantling corporate production, supply, and profit infrastructures through existing governance and regulatory tools. The framework conceptualizes the industry as an ecosystem spanning corporate structures, product categories, supply chains, science distortion, and political influence. Each domain is mapped to disruption levers and institutions, with the aim of reducing implementation risk and limiting industry adaptation. Abolition is framed as a coordinated governance project across local, national, and global levels, with Indigenous peoples and young people recognized as leaders shaping accountability, prevention pathways, and norms. This approach illustrates how abolition-oriented reform may be administratively feasible, legally defensible, and relevant to advancing health equity.

title: Pulmonary nodules: classification, biomarkers, signaling pathways, diseases, early diagnosis and management.
authors: Ye Z, Li L, Zhang M et al.
abstract: Pulmonary nodules are increasingly detected by thoracic imaging and low-dose computed tomography-based lung cancer screening, but most are benign, transient, or indolent. Clinically, the key task is to distinguish nodules that require timely cancer-directed evaluation from those that can be safely observed. This review summarizes the classification, disease spectrum, risk assessment, early diagnosis, biomarkers, signaling mechanisms, translational models, and management of pulmonary nodules. We first distinguish imaging phenotypes and disease entities, then differentiate the individual-level models used to select candidates for lung cancer screening from the nodule-level models and structured reporting systems used after nodule detection. Low-dose computed tomography remains the foundation of screening and surveillance approaches, whereas magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography, contrast-enhanced computed tomography, nonsurgical biopsy, surgical diagnosis, and local therapies play more selective roles depending on the probability of malignancy and patient fitness. Noninvasive biomarkers, including circulating cellular, nucleic acid, methylation, protein, autoantibody, extracellular vesicle, and metabolic analytes, are most likely to serve as adjuncts to imaging and clinical risk assessment rather than as stand-alone diagnostic tests. Artificial intelligence may support detection, workflow efficiency, malignancy risk reclassification, invasiveness assessment, and multimodal integration, but its value depends on external validation, calibration, implementation, and prospective evidence of management benefit. Mechanistic studies of adenocarcinoma spectrum subsolid nodules have implicated the involvement of early oncogenic signaling, genomic instability, immune escape, stromal and vascular remodeling, and adaptive survival pathways. Translational models can support mechanistic and procedural research, but do not replicate real-world nodule management in patients. Overall, care for pulmonary nodules should be risk-adapted, longitudinal, multidisciplinary, and patient-centered.

title: Extreme, Accumulated, and Lagged Exposure to Fire-Sourced PM2.5 and Site-specific Cancer Risk in China.
authors: Zhu H, Pan J, Li Z et al.
abstract: Fire-sourced fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is a chemically distinct component of ambient air pollution, but its association with site-specific cancer risk remains poorly understood. Here we examine associations between fire-sourced PM2.5 and multiple site-specific cancers across China using lagged, accumulated and extreme exposure metrics, and compare them with those for all-source PM2.5. Fire-sourced PM2.5 is positively associated with several cancers, although the pattern varies by exposure metric and cancer site. Lagged and accumulated exposures show the broadest associations, particularly for thyroid, kidney, breast, lung, leukemia and lymphoma cancers, whereas extreme exposure shows a narrower pattern, with the strongest association for laryngeal cancer. Compared with all-source PM2.5, fire-sourced PM2.5 shows stronger and more consistent associations with thyroid, kidney, laryngeal, lymphoma and oral cancers, suggesting that total PM2.5 mass may obscure source-specific cancer risks. Associations are stronger for thyroid and lung cancers in females and for kidney cancer in males, and are generally more pronounced in northern regions and in areas with lower gross domestic product (GDP) or lower tertiary-industry share. These findings identify fire-sourced PM2.5 as a distinct cancer-related exposure and support source-specific and health promotion-oriented air-pollution control strategies, particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged regions.

title: Residential radon in Peru: challenges for health surveillance and lung cancer prevention.
authors: Ordoñez-Aquino C, Venegas Ojeda D, De La Cruz-Vargas JA et al.
journal: Rev Peru Med Exp Salud Publica
abstract: Radon is a globally recognized lung carcinogen and one of the main risk factors for lung cancer in nonsmokers. In Peru, recent evidence indicates elevated radon concentrations in homes in Metropolitan Lima and a possible contribution to the increase in lung cancer, especially in women, although national evidence primarily comes from ecological studies and is still insufficient to establish causality. Regulatory, technical, and surveillance gaps persist that hinder its control. This special article presents a narrative review of international and national evidence and aims to examine the current situation of radon exposure in Peru, identify the regulatory and surveillance gaps that limit its control, and propose specific mitigation measures aligned with international recommendations.

title: The use of TF-Ag-α to selectively capture tumor-derived extracellular vesicles and enhance the predictive performance of extracellular vesicle PD-L1 for response to immune checkpoint inhibitors.
authors: Hsu CC, Qi M, Ito F et al.
abstract: Only a subset of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients benefits from immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Tissue PD-L1 has limited accuracy in predicting ICI response and requires invasive biopsies, highlighting the urgent need for reliable, minimally invasive biomarkers. Extracellular vesicle PD-L1 (EV PD-L1) is a promising liquid biopsy marker, but its predictive performance is confounded by PD-L1 derived from non-tumor cells. We developed a tumor-specific EVs-based assay to predict ICI response. Tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (TEXs) were selectively captured using the tumor-specific Thomsen-Friedenreich glycoantigen alpha (TF-Ag-α), and PD-L1 levels in TEXs expressing TF-Ag-α (i.e., TEXTF-Ag-α PD-L1) were measured in sera from 91 NSCLC patients receiving anti-PD-1 therapy (40 responders and 51 non-responders). Predictive performance was evaluated at pre-treatment baseline, at the end of first treatment cycle, and via fold changes. At pre-treatment baseline, TEXTF-Ag-α PD-L1 showed moderate predictive ability (AUC: 0.76; sensitivity: 0.97; specificity: 0.56). By the end of the first treatment cycle, responders exhibited a ~4.18-fold increase in TEXTF-Ag-α PD-L1 expression, whereas non-responders showed an approximate 20% decrease. Dynamic fold changes after the first treatment cycle substantially improved predictive performance, achieving an AUC of 0.93, sensitivity of 0.95, and specificity of 0.80 for distinguishing responders from non-responders, outperforming both total EV PD-L1 and tissue PD-L1. These results demonstrated that selective TEX capture using TF-Ag-α significantly enhanced the predictive value of EV PD-L1. Dynamic changes in TEXTF-Ag-α PD-L1 provided a highly accurate, minimally invasive biomarker for early assessment of anti-PD-1 response, supporting tumor-specific EVs-based liquid biopsy for precision immunotherapy.

title: Pulmonary dirofilariasis mimicking malignant pulmonary lesions: Two cases presenting as solitary and multiple pulmonary nodules.
authors: Ishihara T, Nakagawa T, Kishi H et al.
abstract: Pulmonary dirofilariasis is a relatively rare zoonotic infection caused by Dirofilaria immitis, which often presents as pulmonary nodules mimicking primary lung cancer or metastatic disease on imaging. Herein, we report two cases of pulmonary dirofilariasis diagnosed using video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection. A man in his 60s with an 8-mm solitary pulmonary nodule and a woman in her 70s with multiple pulmonary nodules detected during follow-up after endoscopic submucosal dissection for intramucosal colorectal cancer underwent thoracoscopic wedge resection because malignancy could not be excluded. 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT) demonstrated only mild or absent fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the lesions. Histopathological examination revealed cross sections of D. immitis within the pulmonary arteries, confirming the diagnosis of pulmonary dirofilariasis in both cases. As pulmonary dirofilariasis closely resembles malignant pulmonary lesions on imaging, preoperative diagnosis remains difficult. Accordingly, this disease should be included in the differential diagnosis of solitary and multiple pulmonary nodules. Video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection provides a valuable approach as it provides definitive diagnosis and curative treatment.

title: A structural dose-response relationship between lymph node yield and survival after anatomical segmentectomy for early-stage NSCLC: a SEER-based retrospective cohort study.
authors: Tian Y, Zanfrini E, Abdelnour-Berchtold E et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate lymph node evaluation is central to oncologic segmentectomy for early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet the quantitative relationship between lymph node yield and survival remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the association between regional lymph node yield and overall survival after segmentectomy for early-stage NSCLC.
METHODS: Using Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) (2000-2022), we identified patients with NSCLC undergoing anatomical segmentectomy and clinical N0M0 disease with tumors ≤30 mm. Regional lymph node yield ("regional nodes examined") was analyzed as 0, 1-5, 6-10, and >10 nodes, and continuously using restricted cubic splines. Overall survival (OS) was evaluated with Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox regression. Lung cancer-specific death was assessed using Fine-Gray competing-risk models.
RESULTS: A total of 2,217 patients met inclusion criteria (median follow-up 58 months), with 783 deaths during follow-up. OS differed significantly across lymph node yield groups (log-rank P<0.001). Five-year OS increased stepwise with higher yield, from 52.5% for 0 nodes to 65.9% for 1-5 nodes, 77.4% for 6-10 nodes, and 83.9% for >10 nodes. In multivariable Cox models, higher yields were independently associated with lower all-cause mortality: 1-5 nodes, hazard ratio (HR) =0.79 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.67-0.94]; 6-10 nodes, HR =0.55 (95% CI: 0.44-0.70), and >10 nodes, HR =0.40 (95% CI: 0.30-0.52) (all P≤0.006; P for trend <0.001). Restricted cubic spline analysis supported a continuous association between yield and mortality risk without strong evidence of non-linearity (P overall <0.001; P non-linearity =0.27). The association was consistent across age (<70 vs. ≥70 years) and tumor size strata (T1a-c), without significant interaction.
CONCLUSIONS: In SEER patients undergoing anatomical segmentectomy for clinical N0M0 NSCLC ≤30 mm, higher regional lymph node yield demonstrated a dose-response association with higher OS and lower lung cancer-specific mortality. These findings support lymph node yield as a pragmatic marker of nodal evaluation during segmentectomy.

title: Prospective Phase II Study of Concurrent Radiotherapy Combined With Full-Course Immunotherapy or Consolidation Immunotherapy for Locally Advanced NSCLC
summary: This is a prospective, randomized phase II study evaluating concurrent chemoradiotherapy combined with full-course immunotherapy or consolidative immunotherapy in patients with unresectable, locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer.

title: Cancer Risk in Patients With Overall and Site-Specific Lichen Planus.
authors: Medianfar CE, Kaderly Rasmussen EL, Baandrup L et al.
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: The association between lichen planus (LP) and subsequent cancer risk, particularly by anatomical site, is not well established.
OBJECTIVE: To assess the association between any LP, and site-specific LP, and the subsequent risk of cancer compared to the general population.
DESIGN, SETTINGS, AND PARTICIPANTS: This was a retrospective cohort study using nationwide Danish register-based data of individuals with an incident LP diagnosis (1978-2020), with no prior cancer, identified through the National Patient Register (any LP) and the Danish Pathology Register (any LP and site-specific LP). Data were analyzed from August 20 to December 20, 2025.
EXPOSURES: Any diagnosis of LP independent of site, and LP at specific anatomical sites (oral, cutaneous, and genital).
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Participants were followed up for incident cancer outcomes until death, emigration, or December 31, 2023. Cancers were identified through the Danish Cancer Register. Standardized incidence ratios (SIRs) with 95% CIs were calculated separately for females and males, comparing cancer incidence in patients with LP to the general Danish female or male population.
RESULTS: A total of 35 845 patients with LP (21 650 females and 14 195 males) were included in the analysis. Compared to the general population, females with any LP had increased risk of oral cancers (lip, SIR = 6.0; 95% CI, 3.3-10.0; oral cavity, SIR = 7.5; 95% CI, 6.4-8.9; tongue, SIR = 6.8; 95% CI, 5.4-8.4) and vulvar cancer (SIR = 2.6; 95% CI, 2.0-3.4), while the risk of squamous cell carcinoma was slightly elevated (SIR = 1.4; 95% CI, 1.3-1.6). In contrast, lung cancer risk was decreased (SIR = 0.7; 95% CI, 0.6-0.8). Results were consistent across follow-up. The cancer risk pattern was similar in male patients with LP. Site-specific analyses showed the highest risk of oral cancers in patients with oral LP, and of genital cancer in patients with genital LP. The 20-year absolute risks in female and male patients were 0.8% (95% CI, 0.7%-1.0%) and 1.0% (95% CI, 0.8-1.2) for oral cavity cancers, 0.5% (95% CI, 0.4%-0.6%) and 0.6% (95% CI, 0.5%-0.8%) for tongue cancers, 0.1% (95% CI, 0%-0.1%) and 0.2% (95% CI, 0.1%-0.3%) for lip cancers, and 0.4% (95% CI, 0.2%-0.5%) and 0.2% (95% CI, 0.1%-0.2%) for genital cancers, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this cohort study, LP was associated with markedly increased risks of oral and genital cancers, as well as a slightly increased risk of skin cancer, particularly at sites corresponding to the anatomical LP location. While the absolute risk is low, site-specific cancer should be considered a possible long-term complication of LP.

title: Thymic epithelial tumors: what's next?
authors: Zhang L, Zhang F, Ismail M et al.
abstract: Thymic epithelial tumors (TETs) are rare malignancies arising in an organ central to T cell development and immune tolerance, creating a distinctive interface between tumor biology and immunotherapy. Complete surgical resection remains the mainstay for resectable disease, whereas systemic treatment options for unresectable, recurrent, and metastatic TETs remain limited. The unique immunobiology of thymoma, particularly impaired central immune tolerance, may account for the unusual balance between antitumor activity and severe immune-related adverse events observed with immune checkpoint blockade. Recent molecular and immune profiling has begun to reveal biologically distinct TET subtypes and potential therapeutic vulnerabilities, including alterations in cell-cycle, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RTK/RAS/MAPK, and DNA damage-response pathways, as well as epigenetic and immune regulatory mechanisms. Emerging strategies, including antibody-drug conjugates and biomarker-informed targeted and immune therapies, may expand systemic treatment options for advanced disease. This review examines these developments in the context of the distinctive biology of the thymus and highlights the key unanswered questions that may shape the next generation of TET research and treatment.

title: Effectiveness of Thymectomy in Alleviating Myasthenia Gravis Symptoms: A Two-Decade Multicenter Experience from Pakistan.
authors: Nabi MS, Naeem M, Sarwar Z et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Thymectomy is an established therapeutic option for myasthenia gravis (MG), but long-term outcomes and predictors of remission from low- and middle-income countries remain limited. This study reports a 20-year, two-center experience evaluating surgical outcomes, neurological improvement, and prognostic factors following thymectomy.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 455 patients with MG who underwent thymectomy between January 2005 and December 2024 at two tertiary centers in Lahore, Pakistan. Neurological outcomes were assessed using the Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America Post-Intervention Status. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify predictors of favorable outcomes, defined as complete stable remission (CSR) or pharmacologic remission.
RESULTS: The mean age was 36.8 ± 13.1 years, with a female predominance (62.4%). Transsternal thymectomy was performed in 63.1% of patients and video-assisted thoracoscopic in 36.9%. Thymic hyperplasia was the most common pathology (55.2%), followed by thymoma (37.8%). At a mean follow-up of 74 ± 38 months, symptomatic improvement was achieved in 85.3% of patients. CSR and pharmacologic remission were observed in 31.2% and 24.6% of patients, respectively. Medication requirements declined significantly postoperatively ( P < 0.001). Five-year recurrence-free survival was 93.2%, and overall survival was 96.4%. Multivariate analysis identified shorter disease duration (<24 months) and non-thymomatous pathology as independent predictors of favorable neurological outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: Thymectomy was associated with durable neurological improvement and a significant reduction in medication dependence among patients with MG. Early surgical intervention, particularly in patients with non-thymomatous disease, was associated with better long-term outcomes, while minimally invasive approaches offered comparable efficacy with reduced perioperative morbidity.

title: A Classic Cutaneous Presentation of Thymoma-Associated Multiorgan Autoimmunity and Review of the Literature.
authors: Fliorent R, Gershman A, Magro C
abstract: Thymoma-associated multiorgan autoimmunity (TAMA) is a rare paraneoplastic syndrome characterized by graft-versus-host disease (GVHD)-like manifestations. The disorder is thought to arise from a disruption to central immune tolerance of T cells secondary to neoplastic growth of thymic epithelial cells. Thymic epithelial cells are crucial in T-cell education: distinguishing between self-antigens and foreign antigens. This process relies on a protein, the autoimmune regulator (AIRE), which negatively selects and eliminates T cells that are self-reactive. With neoplastic transformation of thymic cells, these cells may exhibit reduced AIRE, leading to an overabundance of autoreactive T cells. These autoreactive T cells mediate the sequelae of the GVHD-like presentation, with skin, liver, and gastrointestinal tract manifestations. We describe a case of a 74-year-old patient with a medical history of thymoma and multiple autoimmune conditions, who presented for diffuse psoriasiform eruption of the trunk and back. Skin biopsy further revealed epidermal hyperplasia with interface change, extensive dyskeratosis, and numerous apoptotic keratinocytes within parakeratotic scale, including striking involvement of the follicular epithelium. Our patient developed hepatobiliary and cholestasis injury, with rising bilirubin, AST, and ALT levels. Despite therapeutic modifications, his cutaneous and systemic disease progressed, and he died approximately 1 month after the diagnosis of TAMA due to complications of small bowel obstruction. This case highlights the pressing need for heightened clinical suspicion and a multidisciplinary team approach when presented with a thymoma patient.

title: Cytomegalovirus Enteritis after Surgery for Acute Type A Aortic Dissection Complicated by Malperfusion and Thymoma: A Case Report.
authors: Fukuta H, Narita M, Ushioda R et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) enteritis is a potentially life-threatening gastrointestinal infection typically observed in immunocompromised individuals, such as transplant recipients or patients receiving chemotherapy or long-term corticosteroids. However, CMV enteritis can also develop in the absence of overt immunosuppression, particularly in elderly or critically ill patients under physiological stress, nutritional decline, or prolonged hospitalization. Diagnosis in these settings is challenging because clinical symptoms and imaging findings are nonspecific and may overlap with ischemic or other infectious enteritis.
CASE PRESENTATION: We report a rare case of CMV enteritis in a 65-year-old man who underwent emergent surgical repair for acute type A aortic dissection complicated by superior mesenteric artery (SMA) malperfusion. He underwent total arch replacement, aortic valve replacement with a bioprosthetic valve, and concomitant thymectomy for an anterior mediastinal mass. On POD 4, additional endovascular interventions were performed, including thoracic endovascular aortic repair and SMA stenting. His postoperative course was notable for persistent ileus, poor oral intake, progressive nutritional deterioration, and sustained postoperative fever with elevated inflammatory markers. Because these symptoms and inflammatory findings persisted without an identified infectious source, CMV testing was performed on POD 20. The results, which became available on POD 23, showed positive CMV antigenemia (C7-HRP: 42/50000 WBC) and CMV DNA (1.2 × 104 IU/mL). Abdominal CT demonstrated diffuse small-bowel wall thickening and submucosal edema. Because of his clinical status, endoscopic biopsy was deferred, and CMV enteritis was diagnosed presumptively based on clinical, radiologic, and virologic findings. Intravenous ganciclovir (300 mg every 12 hours) was initiated and continued for 22 days, resulting in gradual improvement in abdominal symptoms, a marked decrease in CMV DNA levels, and conversion of CMV antigenemia to negative. He was transferred to another facility on POD 90.
CONCLUSIONS: CMV enteritis should be considered as a cause of unexplained postoperative fever after open-heart surgery, particularly following repair of acute aortic dissection complicated by malperfusion-related intestinal ischemia, even without classic immunosuppressive conditions. Surgical stress, ischemic bowel injury, and delayed nutritional recovery may predispose critically ill postoperative patients to CMV reactivation. Early CMV testing and timely antiviral therapy may facilitate diagnosis and help prevent clinical deterioration.
